reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant syndrome most often caused by germline loss-of-function variants in PTCH1, a negative regulator of the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway; SUFU variants are a less common cause
Multiple basal cell carcinomas develop from a young age, often on sun-exposed and non-exposed skin, and may number in the many across a lifetime
Odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw are an early and characteristic feature, frequently causing swelling or being found incidentally on dental imaging
Palmar and plantar pits are a useful clinical clue on close skin examination
Skeletal anomalies include bifid or splayed ribs, and calcification of the falx cerebri is commonly seen on skull imaging
There is markedly increased radiosensitivity, so diagnostic and therapeutic radiation should be minimised to avoid inducing new basal cell carcinomas in the treatment field
Childhood medulloblastoma (desmoplastic subtype) occurs in a minority and is an important early risk, particularly with SUFU variants
reference.pathophysiology: Gorlin syndrome arises from germline inactivating variants in PTCH1 (or less often SUFU), key components of the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway. PTCH1 normally inhibits the transmembrane protein Smoothened; loss of PTCH1 function releases this inhibition, leading to constitutive hedgehog pathway activation and unchecked proliferation in susceptible tissues. As a tumour-suppressor mechanism, tumour formation follows a somatic second hit. Aberrant hedgehog signalling explains the developmental anomalies and the predisposition to basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts and medulloblastoma. The same pathway dependence underlies the therapeutic use of hedgehog pathway inhibitors in advanced disease.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic multiple basal cell carcinomas from chronic sun exposure
Xeroderma pigmentosum with early skin cancers
additionalInvestigations: Germline molecular genetic testing of PTCH1 and SUFU including deletion/duplication analysis
Orthopantomogram or jaw imaging for odontogenic keratocysts
Skull and skeletal radiographs for falx calcification and rib or vertebral anomalies
Dermatological mapping and biopsy of suspicious skin lesions
Baseline and clinically guided brain MRI in young children for medulloblastoma surveillance, favouring non-ionising imaging
Cardiac and ovarian ultrasound where fibromas are suspected
redFlags: New neurological signs in a young child raising concern for medulloblastoma
Rapidly enlarging or aggressive basal cell carcinoma, particularly around the eyes, nose or ears
Expanding jaw swelling or pathological fracture from an odontogenic keratocyst
Extensive prior therapeutic radiotherapy given before the diagnosis was recognised
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually near normal, but lifelong burden from recurrent basal cell carcinomas and jaw cysts is considerable and requires ongoing surveillance and treatment. Medulloblastoma in early childhood is the most serious potential complication and drives paediatric monitoring.
pitfalls: Using radiotherapy for basal cell carcinomas and thereby inducing numerous new tumours in the irradiated field
Dismissing multiple early-onset basal cell carcinomas as ordinary sun damage
Missing palmar and plantar pits and jaw cysts that would prompt the diagnosis
Failing to counsel on sun protection and to arrange paediatric medulloblastoma awareness
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
GeneReviews: Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome
management: Complete surgical excision of basal cell carcinomas, using Mohs micrographic surgery where tissue-sparing precision is needed, supplemented by topical or field therapies (imiquimod, photodynamic therapy) for superficial lesions
Reserve hedgehog pathway inhibitors (vismodegib or sonidegib) for extensive, multiple or inoperable basal cell carcinomas exploiting the underlying Smoothened dysregulation
Rigorous photoprotection with sun avoidance and broad-spectrum sunscreen to limit induction of new basal cell carcinomas
Minimise ionising radiation for both diagnosis and treatment given marked radiosensitivity, favouring MRI and ultrasound over CT and radiotherapy
Enucleation or marsupialisation of odontogenic keratocysts with regular orthopantomogram surveillance for recurrence
Lifelong dermatological skin mapping and paediatric brain MRI surveillance for medulloblastoma in early childhood
Coordinate care across dermatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery, paediatric oncology and clinical genetics
Offer genetic counselling and predictive PTCH1/SUFU testing to at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
